title: Precedent and Judicial Reasoning
text:
Precedent, or stare decisis, obliges lower courts to follow the reasoning of higher tribunals on materially identical questions, yet the doctrine is seldom applied mechanically. Judges must first distinguish the ratio decidendi, the principle necessary to the outcome, from obiter dicta, remarks that are persuasive at most. A court confronted with novel facts may therefore reason by analogy, extending a principle to circumstances its originators never contemplated. Critics contend that this latitude invites judicial discretion masquerading as neutral reasoning.

Proponents of the doctrine counter that predictability is itself a form of justice, since citizens who arrange their affairs must be able to anticipate how a dispute would be resolved. Constitutional adjudication complicates matters further, because interpretive methods such as originalism and living constitutionalism often yield divergent readings of identical text. The resulting tension is not merely academic; it shapes whether legal change emerges from legislatures or from the gradual accretion of judicial decisions. Scholars therefore remain divided on whether the common law's adaptability is a virtue or an unacknowledged source of uncertainty.

questions.text: According to the passage, what distinguishes the ratio decidendi from obiter dicta?
options: The ratio decidendi is necessary to the outcome, whereas obiter dicta are merely persuasive
The ratio decidendi binds only the parties, whereas obiter dicta bind all courts
Obiter dicta are issued by legislatures, while the ratio decidendi is issued by juries
The ratio decidendi is always written in Latin

questions.text: According to the proponents mentioned in the second paragraph, why is predictability valuable?
options: It guarantees that every judge reaches the same conclusion
It allows citizens to anticipate how disputes would be resolved
It removes the need for constitutional interpretation
It shortens the time legislatures need to pass laws

questions.text: The passage implies that critics of analogical reasoning are most concerned that:
options: judges will refuse to consider novel facts
personal judgment may be disguised as impartial reasoning
higher courts will ignore precedent entirely
citizens will stop arranging their affairs

questions.text: What can be inferred about the author's view of the debate over the common law?
options: The author considers the question settled in favour of predictability
The author treats the matter as genuinely unresolved among scholars
The author believes legislatures should abandon case law completely
The author rejects originalism as incoherent

freedom to make decisions using one's own judgment

paragraph_translations: O precedente, ou stare decisis, obriga os tribunais inferiores a seguir o raciocínio dos tribunais superiores em questões materialmente idênticas, mas a doutrina raramente é aplicada de forma mecânica. Os juízes devem primeiro distinguir a ratio decidendi, o princípio necessário ao resultado, dos obiter dicta, observações que são, no máximo, persuasivas. Um tribunal diante de fatos inéditos pode, portanto, raciocinar por analogia, estendendo um princípio a circunstâncias que seus criadores jamais previram. Os críticos sustentam que essa margem de liberdade convida à discricionariedade judicial disfarçada de raciocínio neutro.

Os defensores da doutrina respondem que a previsibilidade é, em si, uma forma de justiça, pois os cidadãos que organizam seus negócios devem ser capazes de antecipar como um litígio seria resolvido. A adjudicação constitucional complica ainda mais a questão, porque métodos interpretativos como o originalismo e o constitucionalismo vivo frequentemente produzem leituras divergentes de um mesmo texto. A tensão resultante não é meramente acadêmica; ela define se a mudança jurídica surge dos legislativos ou do acúmulo gradual de decisões judiciais. Os estudiosos permanecem divididos quanto a saber se a adaptabilidade do common law é uma virtude ou uma fonte não reconhecida de incerteza.
